title: Neck and Back Pain from Desk Work: Posture, Breaks and Simple Exercises
metaDescription: Desk work can strain the neck and back. Learn simple desk set-up tips, how often to take breaks, easy exercises and when pain needs a doctor.
intro: Long hours at a desk can strain the neck and back, mostly because the body stays in one position for too long. The most useful steps are to set up your desk sensibly, to move for a few minutes every hour, and to stay physically active. Simple stretches can help. If pain continues beyond a few weeks, or comes with tingling, weakness or other warning signs, get it checked.

sections.heading: Why does desk work cause neck and back pain?
sections.body: Versus Arthritis lists poor posture and lack of exercise among the common contributors to back pain. Lack of exercise can stiffen the spine and weaken the muscles that support it. Versus Arthritis also advises avoiding awkward positions for long periods. Often there is no single cause. Leaning towards a screen or sitting for hours without a break adds to the strain.

sections.heading: How should I set up my desk?
sections.body: An NHS guide for desk-based jobs gives a simple checklist. Try different positions to find what suits you.
bullets: Sit well back in the chair with your lower back supported, both feet flat on the floor and hips level with or slightly above your knees.
Place the screen about an arm's length away, with the top of the screen level with your eyes.
Keep your arms relaxed, forearms roughly level, with the keyboard and mouse within easy reach.
If you use a laptop for more than 15 to 20 minutes, add a separate keyboard and a laptop stand.
Avoid slouching or perching on the front edge of the seat.

sections.heading: How often should I take a break?
sections.body: The NHS guide suggests short regular breaks of five to 10 minutes every hour, rather than fewer long ones. Stand up, walk around or change task. Try not to eat lunch at your desk, and take a short walk instead. Versus Arthritis advises changing your position often and avoiding awkward positions for long periods. Too much rest can make back pain worse.

sections.heading: Which simple exercises help?
sections.body: Stretches can be done at your desk. The NHS guide suggests holding each stretch for 20 seconds and repeating it three times. Stop if you feel pain or tingling.
bullets: Chest stretch: open your arms to the sides with thumbs up and gently squeeze your shoulder blades together, shoulders down.
Chair twist: cross your arms over your chest and turn your upper body and head to each side, feet flat.
Wall press: place your palms on a wall at shoulder height, step back slightly and lean in by bending your elbows. Do three sets of 10.
Walk, swim, or try yoga or Pilates, as these may ease back pain. Start gently and build up.

sections.heading: What if the pain does not settle?
sections.body: Our usual approach starts with medicines for pain. Versus Arthritis says paracetamol and anti-inflammatory tablets such as ibuprofen can be used for about a week to 10 days, taken regularly. The NHS notes that ibuprofen is not suitable for everyone and that paracetamol alone is not recommended for back pain. Once pain eases, exercises and strengthening are the next step, and they work best once pain has settled. Physiotherapy treatments such as ultrasound, short-wave or TENS may be tried for pain relief only. The evidence is modest, and NICE advises against offering TENS and ultrasound for low back pain. Injections are for selected patients. Surgery is the last step, and the decision is yours.

sections.heading: When should I see a doctor?
sections.body: The NHS advises seeing a doctor if pain has not improved after a few weeks of home care, if it stops you doing daily activities, or if you are struggling to cope. Get prompt help for any of these:
bullets: Pain, tingling, weakness or numbness in the arms or legs
Numbness around the genitals or back passage, or changes in bladder or bowel control
Feeling hot, cold, shivery or generally unwell with the pain
Pain that is worse at night or does not ease with rest
Pain that started after a serious accident

faqs.q: What is the correct sitting posture?
faqs.a: Sit well back with your lower back supported, feet flat, and the top of the screen level with your eyes. No posture is right for hours, so change position often.

faqs.q: How long can I sit before moving?
faqs.a: An NHS guide suggests a break of five to 10 minutes every hour. Standing, walking or changing task all count.
Not necessarily. The NHS guide says most standard chairs and desks suit most people. Alternating tasks and moving regularly matters more.

faqs.q: Should I rest if my back hurts?
faqs.a: Short rest is fine, but staying active is advised. Too much rest can make back pain worse.

faqs.q: Do I need a scan for desk-related pain?
faqs.a: Usually not. A scan is considered if you have warning signs, such as weakness or numbness, or if pain does not settle.

faqs.q: Can exercise make the pain worse?
faqs.a: Mild discomfort during exercise is normal and should ease within a few minutes after you finish. Severe pain you cannot cope with means you should see a doctor.
